title: Nettle's Brave Shout
markdown:
Nettle the bunny loved blackberries. He usually munched them near his favorite oak, his fur often dusted purple. Cora the hedgehog, his quick friend, sorted colorful pebbles beside him. High above, Flint the kestrel watched over their home, Whispering Valley.

One evening, a strange shimmer flickered on the abandoned hill. Faint, pulsing lights appeared.

What are those, Nettle whispered, his ears twitching. Open spaces always made him feel wobbly. His whiskers quivered. I can’t do it, a thought echoed.

Cora looked up. They weren’t there yesterday, she rumbled. Those lights seem intentional.

Flint landed on the oak. Lanterns, he confirmed. Someone is lighting them.

We should find out, Cora urged, nudging Nettle.

But it’s so far up there, Nettle mumbled, picturing himself exposed and trembling.

I’ll scout ahead, Flint offered. I’ll find the safest path.

With worry and curiosity, they set off. Cora led through undergrowth, Flint circled above, and Nettle followed, ears back, gaze darting. Brambles caught at his fur. The oak fell away behind them. The hill, which he had always treated as a thing to look at and not climb, grew larger with every hop.

As they climbed, the ground grew steeper. The wind whistled, carrying the scent of damp earth. The lanterns glowed brighter, casting dancing shadows. Flint landed beside them. Someone is up there, he reported. The lights are spaced like signals.

Signals for what, Cora asked.

They crept higher, using brambles for cover. Nettle pressed flat, his usual joy for blackberries replaced by unease. The lights weren’t random. A short flash, then a pause, then two quick flashes. A pattern. A code.

They reached a rocky outcrop. From their vantage point, they saw a hunched figure lighting lanterns. It was Bartholomew, an old squirrel with grey fur. He wore a patched waistcoat and used a long stick.

It’s just an old squirrel, Nettle whispered, relieved.

Suddenly Flint tilted his head. A low rumble grew. The sky darkened rapidly. The wind whipped leaves. The air carried the sharp smell of ozone. A fierce storm was brewing.

Bartholomew looked up, his eyes wide. He began flashing his lanterns frantically. He’s signalling about the storm, Cora said. He’s warning us. He’s afraid.

Flint watched Bartholomew. He’s been out here, alone, trying to keep everyone safe, Flint realized.

Bartholomew fumbled a lantern. It slipped and tumbled down the slope, its light winking out. He let out a small cry.

Nettle watched, his heart aching. Bartholomew’s signals grew weaker. He was alone, his warnings fading.

Nettle understood. Bartholomew’s signals were vital, but wouldn’t reach everyone. He looked towards the very top of the hill, a windswept peak higher and more exposed. He’d always avoided it.

I can help, Nettle said, his voice steady.

Cora and Flint looked at him, surprised.

I can go to the very top, Nettle continued, fear replaced by courage. I can use my voice to make his signals louder. I can shout the warning to the whole valley. A brave thought bloomed.

Flint nodded. It’s dangerous, Nettle. The wind is fierce.

I know, Nettle said, his whiskers trembling, not with fear, but determination. But someone has to make sure everyone hears.

With a resolute nod, Nettle scrambled up the steep slope. The wind buffeted him, rain lashed down. He heard Bartholomew’s frantic flashes below. He felt the storm closing in. He pictured the lonely squirrel, and it gave him strength. He smelled the damp earth, felt the slick stones, saw the swirling sky. He climbed, his legs pumping.

He reached the peak. The wind tore at him. Below, Bartholomew’s lanterns were distant flickers. Nettle took a deep breath. He cupped his paws and shouted, his voice clear, Storm coming. Take shelter. The old hill warns you. He shouted again and again.

He saw creatures scurrying for cover. Sheep huddled. Rabbits vanished. Birds flew to trees.

Bartholomew, seeing Nettle’s efforts, flashed his lanterns with renewed vigour. A faint flicker from a distant farm answered. His frantic movements slowed, replaced by weary relief.

As the storm raged, Nettle, soaked and exhausted but standing tall, felt a warmth spread through him. He had faced his fear of heights, of being exposed. He had used his voice to protect his home.

When the storm passed, Nettle, Cora, and Flint went down. Bartholomew sat by his extinguished lanterns, looking at peace. He offered a shy, grateful smile.

Thank you, he whispered. You helped me. You helped the valley.

Nettle, his paws no longer trembling, smiled back. He looked up at the hill. It no longer seemed a place of fear. It was a place he had already stood, and shouted from, and come down from again.
